# `viewport/SDFColliderRenderer.js`

> **Source:** `editor/js/viewport/SDFColliderRenderer.js`

SDFColliderRenderer — GPU SDF Raymarcher for COLLISION detection ================================================================ ARCHITECTURE OVERVIEW — TWO SEPARATE SDF SYSTEMS: 1. COLLISION SDF (THIS FILE): - Purpose: Physics collision detection via per-pixel GPU raymarching. - How it works: A fullscreen triangle is drawn. For every pixel, the fragment shader raymarches through ALL SDF instances (up to 256) using smooth-min blending (smin) to find the surface. - Cost: EXPENSIVE. O(pixels × instances × marchSteps). At 1080p with 132 capsules and 64 steps, that's ~500M SDF evaluations per frame. - When to use: Only for physics queries that need exact SDF distance fields (e.g. particle-body collision, projectile intersection). - Data flow: Viewport.js (entity loop) → addShape() → instanceBuffer (GPU) → WGSL raymarcher → per-pixel distance field 2. VISUAL OVERLAY (Viewport.js + EntityMeshRenderer): - Purpose: Show a semi-transparent "second skin" over the character mesh so the user can see the collision shape approximation. - How it works: getAnimatedBoneShapes() returns current animated bone positions + mesh-measured capsule sizes. Each bone is rendered as a stretched sphere mesh via EntityMeshRenderer instancing. - Cost: CHEAP. One instanced draw call, standard rasterization. No raymarching, no per-pixel SDF evaluation. - When to use: Always, when the "Show Voxel Colliders" toggle is on. - Data flow: SkeletalAnimation.getAnimatedBoneShapes() → Viewport.js → EntityMeshRenderer.renderEntity() (sphere meshes) RENDERING ORDER (in Viewport.js render loop): 1. Entity meshes (opaque)       — entityMeshRenderer.flush() 2. SDF collision pass            — sdfColliderRenderer.render() [THIS] 3. Rope debug spheres            — entityMeshRenderer (rope particles) 4. Bone visual overlay spheres   — entityMeshRenderer (bone capsules) 5. Bone direction indicators     — boneDirectionLineRenderer 6. Gizmos, grid, ground shadow 7. Post-processing               — bloom, tonemap, reconstruction BLEND MODE: This renderer uses ADDITIVE blending (srcAlpha + one) so the SDF overlay adds color on top of whatever was already rendered. This means: - depthWrite: false (don't occlude other geometry) - depthCompare: 'always' (draw over everything) - The underlying mesh remains visible through the SDF SDF functions are defined in spawnable files and compiled dynamically. Now powered by vGPU driver. Supports: - Primitive shapes (sphere, box, cylinder, capsule, torus) - Custom spawnable shapes (gear, star, helix, etc.) - Universal mesh SDF (auto-fit primitives, triangle sampling, 3D baking)

## Notes & Examples

### Editor Extension System

The editor supports extensions via the same Plauna component system as apps. Extensions can add panels, tools, menu items, and hooks into the engine. They run with elevated 'editor' capability granting access to the scene graph, asset database, and build pipeline.

**Example: Editor extension adding a custom panel**
```js
import { Extension } from 'editor/core/Extension.js';
import { Panel } from 'editor/ui/Panel.js';

class TerrainEditor extends Extension {
  id = 'terrain-editor';
  capabilities = ['editor', 'scene'];
  
  activate(context) {
    // Add menu item
    context.menus.add('Tools/Terrain', () => this.open());
    
    // Register tool
    context.tools.register('terrain', {
      icon: 'mountain',
      onSelect: (entity) => this.edit(entity)
    });
  }
  
  open() {
    this.panel = new Panel({
      title: 'Terrain Editor',
      content: this.buildUI()
    });
    context.workspace.addPanel(this.panel);
  }
  
  edit(entity) {
    const terrain = entity.get(TerrainComponent);
    this.panel.bind(terrain);
  }
}

editor.extensions.register(TerrainEditor);
```

**See also:** [Editor Overview](/editor/overview.md)
